ideas.title: The Seat Compression Panic Is Two Years Early
ideas.thesis: The story dominating software markets right now is seat compression: if AI can do five employees' work, companies pay for one license instead of five, and legacy SaaS slowly dies. B2B software stocks dropped 20% in March 2026, and the median enterprise SaaS EV/Revenue multiple sits at 3.4x, down from above 10x at the 2021 peak. I think the direction is right. I think the timing is wrong. Most enterprise software contracts run two to three years. Renewal cycles are only now beginning to turn over at scale. The actual compression will show up in reported revenue starting in 2027 or 2028, not in 2026. What the market has done is price in a structural shift that is still mostly theoretical. What I find harder to dismiss is the genuine bifurcation opening between AI-native platforms trading at 5x to 6.5x revenue and legacy tools being repriced like utilities. The question I keep returning to is whether the investors buying this dip are early, or a full cycle too early.

ideas.title: What $48.3 Million in March Tells Us About MENA's Infrastructure Bet
ideas.thesis: MENA startup funding fell to $941 million in Q1 2026, down 37% year-on-year. March was worse: $48.3 million total, an 85% drop month-on-month, as the US-Israel-Iran conflict intensified and Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz rattled regional supply chains. The standard read is that this is a crisis. What I find harder to dismiss is the counter-signal buried in the same data. Fintech accounted for 46% of all Q1 investment despite the collapse, with 25 startups capturing the largest share of capital in any sector. The UAE alone attracted $625.8 million across 46 deals, while Saudi Arabia, which had more startups funded (57 versus 46), raised only $156.7 million. What the Q1 numbers seem to show is a deliberate sorting. Capital is concentrating into payments infrastructure, embedded finance tools, and cross-border compliance platforms. Consumer apps and logistics are being cut. I think the interesting essay is not about the funding drop. It is about where the money still went, and why.

ideas.title: What Polygon Is Actually Building: The Payments Company Inside the Blockchain
ideas.thesis: Most people I know still think of Polygon as an Ethereum scaling chain. The more I read about what Polygon Labs has done since January 2026, the more I think that framing is outdated. In a single quarter, Polygon acquired Coinme (licensed fiat on/off-ramps) and Sequence (wallet infrastructure) in a deal worth more than $250 million, unveiled the Open Money Stack as a modular payments framework, and began raising up to $100 million in equity for a dedicated stablecoin payments business. Then on April 29, Meta started routing creator payouts in USDC through Polygon's rails in Colombia and the Philippines, with plans to expand to 160 countries by end of year. What Polygon appears to be assembling, fiat access plus compliance plus wallet infrastructure plus on-chain settlement, looks less like a blockchain product and more like a modular payments API that competes with Stripe. This is my attempt to make sense of what Polygon is actually building, and whether the identity as an L2 chain was always just the first chapter.

ideas.title: Circle Is Building the Abstraction Layer That SWIFT Should Have Been
ideas.thesis: On April 8, 2026, Circle launched CPN Managed Payments, a platform that allows banks and payment providers to settle in stablecoins without ever holding or managing digital assets. Circle handles USDC minting, burning, compliance, and all blockchain infrastructure. The partners interact purely in fiat. That sentence is worth sitting with. The surface story is a product launch. The structural story is different. Circle is positioning itself as invisible middleware between legacy fiat systems and on-chain settlement, which is precisely the position SWIFT has held in correspondent banking for 50 years. And unlike SWIFT, which charges member banks an estimated $1.5 billion per year collectively while settling in three to five days, Circle's model settles in seconds across 20-plus blockchains. Stablecoin transaction volumes already exceeded ACH's $6.8 trillion in February 2026, reaching $7.2 trillion. What is not yet clear to me is whether incumbent banks will accept Circle as the infrastructure layer, or whether this abstraction becomes a threat they will eventually try to build themselves.

ideas.title: Pakistan's Diaspora Economy Has a Stablecoin Upgrade Waiting
ideas.thesis: Pakistan has roughly 4.5 million workers in Gulf states. Their remittances are one of Pakistan's primary sources of foreign exchange, and when the US-Israel-Iran conflict began disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the State Bank of Pakistan immediately flagged remittance risk as a macroeconomic concern. On April 17, Saudi Arabia provided an additional $3 billion in direct support and extended a $5 billion debt facility. That is sovereign rescue finance. Below that level, individual migrant workers are still routing wages home through hawala networks or Western Union, at fees of 3 to 7 percent per transfer. The infrastructure to route that money through stablecoins now exists. Rain raised $250 million in January 2026. Circle's CPN platform settles across 20-plus blockchains. Polygon is building out licensed fiat on-ramps into emerging markets. The same month Pakistan was brokering US-Iran ceasefire talks in Islamabad, the stablecoin rails that could transform how 4.5 million diaspora workers send money home were being quietly assembled. Whether those two facts eventually connect is the question I want to think through.
